claim: The fusion pore establishes an initial aqueous connection to the extracellular space with an upper limit of 3 nm.
source: The first aqueous contact between granule lumen and the extracellular space is a narrow fusion pore (upper limit 3 nm; Albillos et al., 1997)
evidence: The claim cites Albillos et al., 1997 as the source for the 3 nm upper limit measurement.

claim: The fusion pore is thought to consist of both lipids and proteins.
source: The first aqueous contact between granule lumen and the extracellular space is a narrow fusion pore (upper limit 3 nm; Albillos et al., 1997) that is thought to consist of both lipids and proteins (Bao et al., 2016; Sharma and Lindau, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bao et al., 2016 and Sharma and Lindau, 2018.

claim: The fusion pore acts as a molecular sieve that allows release of small transmitter molecules such as nucleotides and catecholamines, but traps larger cargo.
source: At this stage, the pore acts as a molecular sieve that allows release of small transmitter molecules such as nucleotides and catecholamines, but traps larger cargo (Obermüller et al., 2005; Barg et al., 2002; MacDonald et al., 2006; Alvarez de Toledo et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The fusion pore is short-lived and flickers between closed and open states.
source: Electrophysiological experiments have shown that the fusion pore is short-lived and flickers between closed and open states, suggesting that mechanisms exist that stabilize this channel-like structure and restrict pore expansion (MacDonald et al., 2006; Hanna et al., 2009; Breckenridge and Almers, 1987; Lollike et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to electrophysiological studies.

claim: The fusion pore can expand irreversibly (termed full fusion), which leads to mixing of granule and plasma membrane and release of the bulkier hormone content.
source: The pore can then expand irreversibly (termed full fusion), which leads to mixing of granule and plasma membrane and release of the bulkier hormone content (Obermüller et al., 2005; Barg et al., 2002; Anantharam et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The fusion pore can close indefinitely to allow the granule to be retrieved, apparently intact, into the cell interior (termed kiss-and-run or cavicapture).
source: Alternatively, the pore can close indefinitely to allow the granule to be retrieved, apparently intact, into the cell interior (termed kiss-and-run or cavicapture) (Obermüller et al., 2005; MacDonald et al., 2006; Taraska et al., 2003; Tsuboi and Rutter, 2003; Shin et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 20–50% of all exocytosis in β-cells are transient kiss-and-run events that do not lead to insulin release.
source: Estimates in β-cells suggest that 20–50% of all exocytosis in β-cells are transient kiss-and-run events that do not lead to insulin release (Obermüller et al., 2005; MacDonald et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies that provide estimates.

claim: Kiss-and-run exocytosis contributes to local signaling within the islet because smaller granule constituents, such as nucleotides, glutamate or GABA, are released even when the fusion pore does not expand.
source: However, kiss-and-run exocytosis contributes to local signaling within the islet because smaller granule constituents, such as nucleotides, glutamate or GABA, are released even when the fusion pore does not expand.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the molecular sieve properties of the fusion pore.

claim: ATP synchronizes β-cells within the islet.
source: Within the islet, ATP synchronizes β-cells (Hellman et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hellman et al., 2004.

claim: ATP has both inhibitory and stimulatory effects on insulin secretion.
source: Within the islet, ATP synchronizes β-cells (Hellman et al., 2004), and has both inhibitory (Salehi et al., 2005; Poulsen et al., 1999) and stimulatory (Richards-Williams et al., 2008) effects on insulin secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies showing different effects.

claim: ATP suppresses glucagon release from α-cells.
source: ATP suppresses glucagon release from α-cells (Tudurí et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tudurí et al., 2008.

claim: ATP activates macrophages.
source: ATP suppresses glucagon release from α-cells (Tudurí et al., 2008), and activates macrophages (Weitz et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Weitz et al., 2018.

claim: Interstitial GABA leads to tonic GABA-A receptor activation and α-cell proliferation.
source: Interstitial GABA leads to tonic GABA-A receptor activation and α-cell proliferation (Jin et al., 2013; Ben-Othman et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jin et al., 2013 and Ben-Othman et al., 2017.

claim: Glutamate stimulates glucagon secretion.
source: glutamate stimulates glucagon secretion (Cabrera et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cabrera et al., 2008.

claim: Pore behavior has been shown to be regulated by cytosolic Ca2+, cAMP, PI(4,5)P2, and activation of protein kinase C (PKC).
source: Pore behavior has been shown to be regulated by cytosolic Ca2+, cAMP, PI(4,5)P2, and activation of protein kinase C (PKC) (MacDonald et al., 2006; Hanna et al., 2009; Alés et al., 1999; Calejo et al., 2013; Scepek et al., 1998)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Elevated Ca2+ and dynamin promote pore closure.
source: recent superresolution imaging indicates that elevated Ca2+ and dynamin promote pore closure (Shin et al., 2018; Chiang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent superresolution imaging studies.

claim: Both myosin and the small GTPase dynamin are involved in fusion pore restriction.
source: Both myosin and the small GTPase dynamin are involved in fusion pore restriction (Jackson et al., 2015; Tsuboi et al., 2004; Graham et al., 2002; Artalejo et al., 1995; Aoki et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Assembly of filamentous actin promotes fusion pore expansion.
source: assembly of filamentous actin promotes fusion pore expansion (Wen et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wen et al., 2016.

claim: In β-cells of type-2 diabetics, upregulation of amisyn leads to decreased insulin secretion because fusion pore expansion is impaired.
source: In β-cells of type-2 diabetics, upregulation of amysin leads to decreased insulin secretion because fusion pore expansion is impaired (Collins et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Collins et al., 2016.

claim: The Parkinson's related protein α-synuclein promotes fusion pore dilation in chromaffin cells and neurons.
source: the Parkinson's related protein α-synuclein promotes fusion pore dilation in chromaffin cells and neurons (Logan et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Logan et al., 2017.

claim: Sulfonylureas close the KATP channel by binding to its regulatory subunit SUR1, which leads to increased electrical activity and Ca2+-influx that triggers insulin secretion.
source: First, sulfonylureas (e.g. tolbutamide and glibenclamide) close the KATP channel by binding to its regulatory subunit SUR1, which leads to increased electrical activity and Ca2+-influx that triggers insulin secretion (Henquin, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Henquin, 2000.

claim: Activation of the receptor for the incretin hormone glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) raises cytosolic [cAMP] and thereby increases the propensity of insulin granules to undergo exocytosis.
source: Second, activation of the receptor for the incretin hormone glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) raises cytosolic [cAMP] and thereby increases the propensity of insulin granules to undergo exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of GLP-1 receptor signaling.

claim: The effect of cAMP on exocytosis is mediated by a protein-kinase A (PKA)-dependent pathway, and by Epac2.
source: The effect of cAMP on exocytosis is mediated by a protein-kinase A (PKA)-dependent pathway, and by Epac2, a guanine nucleotide exchange factor for the Ras-like small GTPase Rap (Kawasaki et al., 1998) that is a direct target for cAMP (Ozaki et al., 2000) and is recruited to insulin granule docking sites (Alenkvist et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Epac2 is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor for the Ras-like small GTPase Rap.
source: Epac2, a guanine nucleotide exchange factor for the Ras-like small GTPase Rap (Kawasaki et al., 1998)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kawasaki et al., 1998.

claim: Epac2 is a direct target for cAMP.
source: Epac2, a guanine nucleotide exchange factor for the Ras-like small GTPase Rap (Kawasaki et al., 1998) that is a direct target for cAMP (Ozaki et al., 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ozaki et al., 2000.

claim: Epac2 is recruited to insulin granule docking sites.
source: Epac2, a guanine nucleotide exchange factor for the Ras-like small GTPase Rap (Kawasaki et al., 1998) that is a direct target for cAMP (Ozaki et al., 2000) and is recruited to insulin granule docking sites (Alenkvist et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Alenkvist et al., 2017.

claim: Epac2 has been suggested to be activated by sulfonylureas.
source: Epac2 has also been suggested to be activated by sulfonylureas (Zhang et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: Activation of Epac2 restricts expansion of the insulin granule fusion pore by recruiting dynamin and amisyn to the exocytosis site.
source: We report that activation of Epac2, either through GLP1-R/cAMP signaling or via sulfonylurea, restricts expansion of the insulin granule fusion pore by recruiting dynamin and amisyn to the exocytosis site.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Activation of Epac2 by two classes of antidiabetic drugs (GLP-1 receptor agonists and sulfonylureas) hinders full fusion and insulin release.
source: Activation of this pathway by two classes of antidiabetic drugs therefore hinders full fusion and insulin release, which is expected to reduce their effectiveness as insulin secretagogues.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: In full fusion events, fluorescence of a granule that was stably situated at the plasma membrane suddenly vanished during stimulation (in most cases within <100 ms).
source: In the first, termed full fusion, fluorescence of a granule that was stably situated at the plasma membrane suddenly vanished during the stimulation (in most cases within <100 ms; Figure 1a–c, left panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1a-c.

claim: The sudden loss of fluorescence in full fusion events is interpreted as rapid pore widening that allowed general release of granule cargo.
source: Since the EGFP label is relatively large (3.7 nm vs 3 nm for insulin monomers), this is interpreted as rapid pore widening that allowed general release of granule cargo.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the size of the EGFP label relative to the fusion pore.

claim: In flash events, the rapid loss of the granule marker was preceded by an increase in its fluorescence that could last for several seconds.
source: In the second type, the rapid loss of the granule marker was preceded by an increase in its fluorescence that could last for several seconds (flash events, Figure 1a–c, right panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1a-c.

claim: The fluorescence increase in flash events reflects neutralization of the acidic granule lumen and dequenching of the EGFP-label, before the labeled cargo is released.
source: We and others have previously shown (Taraska et al., 2003; Ferraro et al., 2005; Gandasi and Barg, 2014) that this reflects neutralization of the acidic granule lumen and dequenching of the EGFP-label, before the labeled cargo is released.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The neutralization in flash events occurs as the result of proton flux through the fusion pore.
source: Since this neutralization occurs as the result of proton flux through the fusion pore, the fluorescence timecourse of these events can be used to quantitatively study fusion pore behavior.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of pH-dependent fluorescence changes.

claim: Forskolin increased the fraction of flash events by nearly twofold.
source: Indeed, when forskolin (2 µM; fsk) was added to the bath solution we observed a twofold increase of exocytosis rate (Figure 1f), a threefold increase of NPY release times (Figure 1e), and a nearly doubled fraction of events with restricted fusion pores (Figure 1d,f).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1d and 1f.

claim: Forskolin increased NPY release times threefold.
source: Indeed, when forskolin (2 µM; fsk) was added to the bath solution we observed a twofold increase of exocytosis rate (Figure 1f), a threefold increase of NPY release times (Figure 1e), and a nearly doubled fraction of events with restricted fusion pores (Figure 1d,f).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Forskolin increased exocytosis rate twofold.
source: Indeed, when forskolin (2 µM; fsk) was added to the bath solution we observed a twofold increase of exocytosis rate (Figure 1f), a threefold increase of NPY release times (Figure 1e), and a nearly doubled fraction of events with restricted fusion pores (Figure 1d,f).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The GLP-1 agonist exendin-4 (10 nM) had comparable effects to forskolin on fusion pore behavior.
source: The GLP-1 agonist exendin-4 (10 nM; Ex4) had comparable effects (Figure 1d–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1d-f.

claim: The effect of forskolin on fusion pore behavior was mimicked by the specific Epac2 agonist S223.
source: The effect of fsk on fusion pore behavior was mimicked by the specific Epac2 agonist S223 (Schwede et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schwede et al., 2015 and experimental data.

claim: Incubation with S223-acetomethoxyester (5 µM) increased the fraction of flash events by 60%.
source: Incubation with S223-acetomethoxyester (5 µM) increased the fraction of flash events by 60% (Figure 1d), doubled average NPY release times (Figure 1e) and doubled the event frequency (Figure 1f)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: S223 doubled average NPY release times.
source: Incubation with S223-acetomethoxyester (5 µM) increased the fraction of flash events by 60% (Figure 1d), doubled average NPY release times (Figure 1e) and doubled the event frequency (Figure 1f)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: S223 doubled the event frequency.
source: Incubation with S223-acetomethoxyester (5 µM) increased the fraction of flash events by 60% (Figure 1d), doubled average NPY release times (Figure 1e) and doubled the event frequency (Figure 1f)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The effects of forskolin and S223 were not additive.
source: the effects of fsk and S223 were not additive.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data comparing combined treatment to individual treatments.

claim: The Epac-inhibitor ESI-09 decreased the exocytosis rate in the presence of forskolin by 80%.
source: In contrast, the Epac-inhibitor ESI-09 decreased the exocytosis rate in the presence of fsk by 80% (Figure 1f)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: ESI-09 reduced the average NPY release time by 60% in the presence of forskolin.
source: the Epac-inhibitor ESI-09 decreased the exocytosis rate in the presence of fsk by 80% (Figure 1f), and the average NPY release time and the fraction of flash events were both reduced by 60% (Figure 1d–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: ESI-09 reduced the fraction of flash events by 60% in the presence of forskolin.
source: the Epac-inhibitor ESI-09 decreased the exocytosis rate in the presence of fsk by 80% (Figure 1f), and the average NPY release time and the fraction of flash events were both reduced by 60% (Figure 1d–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: PKA inhibition with Rp8-Br-cAMPS decreased neither the fraction of flash events, nor average NPY release times.
source: PKA inhibition with Rp8-Br-cAMPS (Gjertsen et al., 1995) decreased neither the fraction of flash events, nor average NPY release times (Figure 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1e and citation to Gjertsen et al., 1995.

claim: Epac rather than PKA is responsible for cAMP-dependent fusion pore regulation.
source: The results indicate that Epac rather than PKA is responsible for cAMP-dependent fusion pore regulation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the differential effects of Epac and PKA inhibitors.

claim: Epac activation increases the rate of exocytosis but slows the rate of peptide release from individual granules.
source: Paradoxically, Epac activation increases the rate of exocytosis but slows the rate of peptide release from individual granules.
evidence: The claim is based on the combined observations of increased exocytosis rate and increased NPY release times.

claim: Epac2 overexpression had no effect on the overall exocytosis rate in either absence or presence of forskolin.
source: Epac2 overexpression had no effect on the overall exocytosis rate in either absence or presence of fsk (Figure 2a)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Epac2 overexpression increased the rate of flash events.
source: Epac2 overexpression had no effect on the overall exocytosis rate in either absence or presence of fsk (Figure 2a), but increased the rate of flash events (Figure 2b–c)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2b-c.

claim: NPY release times in cells overexpressing Epac2 increased threefold in the absence of forskolin.
source: NPY release times in cells overexpressing Epac2 increased threefold in the absence of fsk, and were similar to controls in presence of fsk (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: A high Epac concentration can achieve sufficient activity to affect insulin secretion even at basal cAMP level.
source: This indicates that a high Epac concentration can achieve sufficient activity to affect insulin secretion even at basal cAMP level, likely because cAMP acts in part by increasing the Epac concentration at the plasma membrane (Alenkvist et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the overexpression data and citation to Alenkvist et al., 2017.

claim: Including cAMP in the pipette solution increased the frequency of current spikes by 50%.
source: Including cAMP in the pipette solution increased the frequency of current spikes by 50%, consistent with accelerated exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: The effect of cAMP on current spike frequency was blocked if the Epac inhibitor ESI-09 was present.
source: This effect of cAMP was blocked if the Epac inhibitor ESI-09 was present (Figure 3b–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3b-c.

claim: In the presence of cAMP, current spikes were markedly widened as indicated by on average 20% longer half-widths.
source: In the presence of cAMP, but not cAMP + ESI-09, they were markedly widened as indicated by on average 20% longer half-widths (Figure 3d)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: In the presence of cAMP, current spikes showed 30% longer decay constants.
source: In the presence of cAMP, but not cAMP + ESI-09, they were markedly widened as indicated by on average 20% longer half-widths (Figure 3d), 30% longer decay constants (τ, Figure 3e)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: In the presence of cAMP, current spikes showed 40% slower rising phases.
source: In the presence of cAMP, but not cAMP + ESI-09, they were markedly widened as indicated by on average 20% longer half-widths (Figure 3d), 30% longer decay constants (τ, Figure 3e), and 40% slower rising phases (25–75% slope, Figure 3f)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Nucleotide release is slowed by cAMP, likely because of changed fusion pore kinetics.
source: This indicates that nucleotide release is slowed by cAMP, likely because of changed fusion pore kinetics.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the electrophysiological data.

claim: The cAMP effect on nucleotide release is probably mediated by Epac because it is blocked by ESI-09.
source: Since the effect is blocked by ESI-09, we conclude that the cAMP effect probably is mediated by Epac.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the ESI-09 blocking experiment.

claim: In the absence of forskolin, exocytosis was significantly slower in Epac2-/- cells than WT cells.
source: In the absence of forskolin, exocytosis was significantly slower in Epac2-/- cells than WT cells, and the fraction of flash-associated exocytosis events was five-fold lower (Figure 4c–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 4c-e.

claim: The fraction of flash-associated exocytosis events was five-fold lower in Epac2-/- cells than WT cells in the absence of forskolin.
source: In the absence of forskolin, exocytosis was significantly slower in Epac2-/- cells than WT cells, and the fraction of flash-associated exocytosis events was five-fold lower (Figure 4c–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 4c-e.

claim: Fusion pore life-times were strikingly shorter in Epac2-/- cells compared with WT.
source: This was paralleled by strikingly shorter fusion pore life-times in Epac2-/- cells compared with WT (Figure 4f).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Epac2 is partially activated in hyperglycemic conditions in mouse β-cells.
source: The data suggest that Epac2 is partially activated in these conditions, consistent with elevated cAMP levels in mouse β-cells in hyperglycemic conditions (Dyachok et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the Epac2-/- data and citation to Dyachok et al., 2008.

claim: Forskolin increased both exocytosis and the fraction of flash events of WT cells.
source: As expected, forskolin increased both exocytosis (Figure 4e) and the fraction of flash events (Figure 4c) of WT cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 4c and 4e.

claim: Forskolin failed to accelerate exocytosis in Epac2-/- cells.
source: In contrast, forskolin failed to accelerate exocytosis in Epac2-/- cells, and the fraction of flash events was similar with or without forskolin (Figure 4c,f–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 4c, f-g.

claim: The fraction of flash events was similar with or without forskolin in Epac2-/- cells.
source: In contrast, forskolin failed to accelerate exocytosis in Epac2-/- cells, and the fraction of flash events was similar with or without forskolin (Figure 4c,f–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 4c, f-g.

claim: The effects of cAMP on fusion pore behavior are mediated specifically by Epac2.
source: We conclude therefore that the effects of cAMP on fusion pore behavior are mediated specifically by Epac2.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the Epac2-/- mouse data.

claim: Sulfonylureas have been reported to activate Epac.
source: Sulfonylureas have been reported to activate Epac (Zhang et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: In the absence of forskolin, sulfonylureas accelerated K+-stimulated exocytosis about twofold over that observed in control.
source: In the absence of fsk, the sulfonylureas accelerated K+-stimulated exocytosis about twofold over that observed in control (Figure 5b, left)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Sulfonylureas augment insulin secretion via intracellular targets.
source: In the absence of fsk, the sulfonylureas accelerated K+-stimulated exocytosis about twofold over that observed in control (Figure 5b, left), which is consistent with earlier findings that sulfonylureas augment insulin secretion via intracellular targets (Barg et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Barg et al., 1999.

claim: The effect of sulfonylureas on exocytosis was entirely due to an increase in flash-associated exocytosis events.
source: This effect was entirely due to an increase in flash-associated exocytosis events (Figure 5b–c)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 5b-c.

claim: The average NPY release time increased in the presence of sulfonylurea.
source: the average NPY release time increased accordingly in the presence of sulfonylurea (Figure 5d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Forskolin strongly stimulated both flash-associated and full fusion exocytosis in absence of sulfonylurea.
source: Fsk strongly stimulated both flash-associated and full fusion exocytosis in absence of sulfonylurea (Figure 5b–c, middle)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 5b-c.

claim: Under forskolin conditions, sulfonylureas tended to decrease full-fusion exocytosis without effect on the frequency of flash-associated events.
source: under these conditions, sulfonylureas tended to decrease full-fusion exocytosis without effect on the frequency of flash-associated events (Figure 5b, middle).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: NPY release times were elevated with forskolin compared with control (no forskolin), and only marginally longer than with forskolin alone when sulfonylureas were present.
source: Accordingly, NPY release times were elevated compared with control (no fsk), and only marginally longer than with fsk alone (Figure 5d, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: In human β-cells, glibenclamide increased exocytosis in the absence of forskolin but not in its presence.
source: Similar results were obtained in human β-cells, where glibenclamide increased exocytosis in the absence of fsk (p=0.01, n = 13 cells from four donors) but not in its presence (p=0.80, n = 7 cells from four donors; data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from human β-cells.

claim: Sulfonylureas restrict fusion pore expansion through the same intracellular pathway as cAMP.
source: The data indicate that sulfonylureas restrict fusion pore expansion through the same intracellular pathway as cAMP, which may counteract their stimulating effect on exocytosis by preventing or delaying peptide release.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the similar effects of sulfonylureas and cAMP.

claim: When sulfonylureas were applied acutely, the fraction of flash-associated exocytosis events and the NPY release times were similar to control for all three sulfonylureas.
source: Under these conditions, the fraction of flash-associated exocytosis events (Figure 5f–g) and the NPY release times (Figure 5h) were similar to control (stimulation with elevated K+) for all three sulfonylureas.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 5f-h.

claim: Sulfonylureas must enter the cytosol to affect fusion pore behavior.
source: Taken together, the data suggest that sulfonylureas must enter the cytosol to affect fusion pore behavior, and that this effect is not mediated by the plasma membrane SUR.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the acute vs. chronic application experiments.

claim: The effect of sulfonylureas on fusion pore behavior is not mediated by the plasma membrane SUR.
source: Taken together, the data suggest that sulfonylureas must enter the cytosol to affect fusion pore behavior, and that this effect is not mediated by the plasma membrane SUR.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: An EGFP-tagged SUR1 expressed in INS-1 cells did not localize to exocytosis sites or affect fusion pore behavior.
source: Moreover, an EGFP-tagged SUR1 (EGFP-SUR1) expressed in INS-1 cells did not localize to exocytosis sites or affect fusion pore behavior (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sulfonylureas affect fusion pore behavior through Epac2.
source: We therefore conclude that sulfonylureas affect fusion pore behavior through Epac2.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data.

claim: In the presence of forskolin, both dynamin1 and amisyn were recruited to the granule site during membrane fusion.
source: In the presence of fsk, both of the two fluorescent proteins were recruited to the granule site during membrane fusion (Figure 6c,f, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6c, 6f, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of dynamin1 and amisyn was about 2–4 fold compared with endogenous levels.
source: Expression of both proteins was about 2–4 fold compared with endogenous levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression of dynamin1 and amisyn markedly increased the NPY release times.
source: Expression of both proteins was about 2–4 fold compared with endogenous levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), and markedly increased the NPY release times (Figure 6d, g)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6d and 6g.

claim: Expression of dynamin1 and amisyn increased flash-associated exocytosis events.
source: Expression of both proteins was about 2–4 fold compared with endogenous levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), and markedly increased the NPY release times (Figure 6d, g) and flash-associated exocytosis events (Figure 6e,h).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6e and 6h.

claim: Addition of the Epac inhibitor ESI09 prevented recruitment of both dynamin1 and amisyn during flash events.
source: Addition of the Epac inhibitor ESI09 prevented recruitment of both dynamin1 and amisyn during flash events and reduced flash events and NPY release times below control (Figure 6c–h).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6c-h.

claim: ESI09 reduced flash events and NPY release times below control.
source: Addition of the Epac inhibitor ESI09 prevented recruitment of both dynamin1 and amisyn during flash events and reduced flash events and NPY release times below control (Figure 6c–h).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6c-h.

claim: In the absence of forskolin, expression of dynamin1 and amisyn had no effect on fusion pore behavior.
source: In the absence of fsk, expression of the two proteins had no effect on fusion pore behavior, and only amisyn (but not dynamin1) was recruited to the exocytosis site (Figure 6i–n).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6i-n.

claim: In the absence of forskolin, only amisyn (but not dynamin1) was recruited to the exocytosis site.
source: In the absence of fsk, expression of the two proteins had no effect on fusion pore behavior, and only amisyn (but not dynamin1) was recruited to the exocytosis site (Figure 6i–n).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6i-n.

claim: When Epac was activated with S223 (no forskolin), dynamin1 and amisyn were recruited during flash events.
source: When Epac was activated with S223 (no fsk), dynamin1 and amisyn were recruited during flash events, and NPY release times and flash events were increased for both proteins (Figure 6i–n).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6i-n.

claim: When Epac was activated with S223, NPY release times and flash events were increased for both dynamin1 and amisyn.
source: When Epac was activated with S223 (no fsk), dynamin1 and amisyn were recruited during flash events, and NPY release times and flash events were increased for both proteins (Figure 6i–n).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6i-n.

claim: Dynamin1 and amisyn are acutely recruited to the exocytosis site, where they participate in cAMP-dependent fusion pore restriction.
source: The data suggest that dynamin1 and amisyn are acutely recruited to the exocytosis site, where they participate in cAMP-dependent fusion pore restriction.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the recruitment and functional data.

claim: cAMP-dependent signaling restricts fusion pore expansion and promotes kiss-and-run exocytosis in β-cells.
source: cAMP-dependent signaling restricts fusion pore expansion and promotes kiss-and-run exocytosis in β-cells (Hanna et al., 2009) and neuroendocrine cells (Calejo et al., 2013; Machado et al., 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cAMP-mediator Epac2 orchestrates fusion pore restriction by engaging dynamin and perhaps other endocytosis-related proteins at the release site.
source: We show here that the cAMP-mediator Epac2 orchestrates these effects by engaging dynamin and perhaps other endocytosis-related proteins at the release site (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The fusion pore acts as a molecular sieve, causing insulin and other peptides to remain trapped within the granule, while smaller transmitter molecules with para- or autocrine function are released.
source: Since the fusion pore acts as a molecular sieve, the consequence is that insulin and other peptides remain trapped within the granule, while smaller transmitter molecules with para- or autocrine function are released (Obermüller et al., 2005; MacDonald et al., 2006; Taraska et al., 2003; Leclerc et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and the current findings.

claim: Incretin signaling and Epac activation delays, or altogether prevents insulin secretion from individual granules, while promoting paracrine intra-islet communication.
source: Incretin signaling and Epac activation therefore delays, or altogether prevents insulin secretion from individual granules, while promoting paracrine intra-islet communication that is based mostly on release of small transmitter molecules.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Two clinically important classes of antidiabetic drugs, GLP-1 analogs and sulfonylureas, activate Epac in β-cells and caused restriction of the fusion pore.
source: Paradoxically, two clinically important classes of antidiabetic drugs, GLP-1 analogs and sulfonylureas, activate Epac in β-cells and caused restriction of the fusion pore.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin secretion by binding to SUR1, which results in closure of KATP channels and depolarization.
source: Sulfonylureas have long been known to stimulate insulin secretion by binding to SUR1, which results in closure of KATP channels and depolarization (Henquin, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Henquin, 2000.

claim: Sulfonylureas accelerate PKA-independent granule priming in β-cells, which may involve activation of intracellularly localized SUR1.
source: The drugs also accelerate PKA-independent granule priming in β-cells, which may involve activation of intracellularly localized SUR1 (Eliasson et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Eliasson et al., 2003.

claim: Sulfonylureas exert a third mode of action that leads to the restriction of the fusion pore and therefore limits insulin release.
source: Our data indicate that sulfonylureas exert a third mode of action that leads to the restriction of the fusion pore and therefore limits insulin release.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Acute exposure to sulfonylureas had no effect on fusion pore behavior, although it blocks KATP channels.
source: First, acute exposure to sulfonylureas had no effect on fusion pore behavior, although it blocks KATP channels (indicating SUR1 activation).
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental findings.

claim: Only long-term exposure to sulfonylurea resulted in restricted fusion pores, likely because it allowed the drugs to enter the cytoplasm.
source: Only long-term exposure to sulfonylurea resulted in restricted fusion pores, likely because it allowed the drugs to enter the cytoplasm.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: SUR1 was not detected at enrichment at the granule release site, which precludes any direct role of the protein in fusion pore regulation.
source: Second, we could not detect enrichment of SUR1 at the granule release site, which precludes any direct role of the protein in fusion pore regulation.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental findings.

claim: Sulfonylurea compounds have been shown to allosterically stabilize the cAMP-dependent activation of Epac.
source: Sulfonylurea compounds have been shown to allosterically stabilize the cAMP-dependent activation of Epac (Takahashi et al., 2013; Herbst et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Takahashi et al., 2013 and Herbst et al., 2011.

claim: Basal cAMP concentrations are sufficient for sulfonylurea to cause fusion pore restriction.
source: Our finding that sulfonylurea caused fusion pore restriction in the absence of forskolin indicates that basal cAMP concentrations are sufficient for this effect.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Gliclizide binds the CNB1 domain without activating it.
source: Since gliclizide binds the CNB1 domain without activating it (Takahashi et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Takahashi et al., 2013.

claim: Epac localization at the granule site may be enough to regulate downstream proteins (e.g. dynamin and amisyn).
source: Since gliclizide binds the CNB1 domain without activating it (Takahashi et al., 2013) and still restricts the fusion pore, Epac localization at the granule site (Alenkvist et al., 2017) may be enough to regulate the downstream proteins (e.g. dynamin and amisyn).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings and citations.

claim: The competing stimulatory and inhibitory effects of sulfonylureas on insulin secretion may contribute to the reduction in sulfonylurea effectiveness with time of treatment.
source: It can further be speculated that the competing stimulatory (via exocytosis) and inhibitor effects (via the fusion pore) of sulfonylureas on insulin secretion, contribute to the reduction in sulfonylurea effectiveness with time of treatment.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the experimental findings.

claim: Long-term treatment with GLP-1 analogs disturbs glucose homeostasis.
source: Long-term treatment with GLP-1 analogs disturbs glucose homeostasis (Abdulreda et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Abdulreda et al., 2016.

claim: Combination therapy of sulfonylurea and DPP4 inhibitors has been shown to lead to severe hypoglycemia.
source: combination therapy of sulfonylurea and DPP4 inhibitors (that elevate cAMP) has been shown to lead to severe hypoglycemia (Yabe and Seino, 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yabe and Seino, 2014.

claim: The hypoglycemia from combination therapy of sulfonylurea and DPP4 inhibitors likely depends on Epac.
source: combination therapy of sulfonylurea and DPP4 inhibitors (that elevate cAMP) has been shown to lead to severe hypoglycemia (Yabe and Seino, 2014), an effect that likely depends on Epac (Takahashi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Takahashi et al., 2015.

claim: Epac mediates the PKA-independent stimulation of exocytosis by cAMP.
source: Epac mediates the PKA-independent stimulation of exocytosis by cAMP (Seino et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Seino et al., 2009.

claim: Epac may affect both priming and fusion pore restriction.
source: Epac mediates the PKA-independent stimulation of exocytosis by cAMP (Seino et al., 2009) and our data suggests it may affect both priming and fusion pore restriction.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: The effect of Epac on exocytosis is rapid, suggesting that Epac is preassembled at the site of the secretory machinery.
source: This effect is rapid (Eliasson et al., 2003), suggesting that Epac is preassembled at the site of the secretory machinery.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from citation to Eliasson et al., 2003.

claim: Epac concentrates at sites of docked insulin granules.
source: Indeed, Epac concentrates at sites of docked insulin granules (Alenkvist et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Alenkvist et al., 2017.

claim: Epac forms functionally relevant complexes with the tethering proteins Rim2 and Piccolo.
source: Epac concentrates at sites of docked insulin granules (Alenkvist et al., 2017), and forms functionally relevant complexes with the tethering proteins Rim2 and Piccolo (Fujimoto et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fujimoto et al., 2002.

claim: The amount of Epac2 present at individual release sites did not correlate with fusion pore behavior.
source: However, the amount of Epac2 present at individual release sites did not correlate with fusion pore behavior, which may indicate that the protein acts indirectly by activating or recruiting other proteins.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations.

claim: Epac2 may act indirectly by activating or recruiting other proteins.
source: However, the amount of Epac2 present at individual release sites did not correlate with fusion pore behavior, which may indicate that the protein acts indirectly by activating or recruiting other proteins.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Known targets of Epac are the small GTPases Rap1 and R-Ras, for which Epac is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF).
source: Other known targets of Epac are the small GTPases Rap1 and R-Ras, for which Epac is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of Epac function.

claim: Rap1 is expressed on insulin granules and affects insulin secretion both directly and by promoting intracellular Ca2+-release following phospholipase-C activation.
source: Rap1 is expressed on insulin granules and affects insulin secretion both directly (Shibasaki et al., 2007), and by promoting intracellular Ca2+-release following phospholipase-C activation (Dzhura et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shibasaki et al., 2007 and Dzhura et al., 2011.

claim: R-Ras is an activator of phosphoinositide 3-kinase.
source: R-Ras is an activator of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (Marte et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Marte et al., 1997.

claim: By altering local phosphoinositide levels, Epac could indirectly affect exocytosis via recruitment of C2-domain proteins such as Munc13.
source: By altering local phosphoinositide levels, Epac could therefore indirectly affect exocytosis via recruitment of C2-domain proteins such as Munc13 (Kang et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference and citation to Kang et al., 2006.

claim: By altering local phosphoinositide levels, Epac could affect fusion pore behavior by recruitment of the PH-domain containing proteins dynamin and amisyn.
source: By altering local phosphoinositide levels, Epac could therefore indirectly affect exocytosis via recruitment of C2-domain proteins such as Munc13 (Kang et al., 2006), and fusion pore behavior by recruitment of the PH-domain containing proteins dynamin and amisyn (Ramachandran and Schmid, 2008; Abbineni et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference and citations.

claim: Dynamin causes vesicle fission during clathrin-dependent endocytosis.
source: Dynamin causes vesicle fission during clathrin-dependent endocytosis (Marks et al., 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Marks et al., 2001.

claim: Dynamin is present at the exocytosis site and required for the kiss-and-run mode.
source: since dynamin is present at the exocytosis site and required for the kiss-and-run mode (Jackson et al., 2015; Tsuboi et al., 2004; Trexler et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Dynamin may have a similar role during transient exocytosis as it does during endocytosis.
source: since dynamin is present at the exocytosis site and required for the kiss-and-run mode (Jackson et al., 2015; Tsuboi et al., 2004; Trexler et al., 2016), it may have a similar role during transient exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the known role of dynamin.

claim: Granules lose some of their membrane proteins during transient exocytosis.
source: An active scission mechanism is also suggested by the finding that granules loose some of their membrane proteins during transient exocytosis (Tsuboi et al., 2004; Perrais et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tsuboi et al., 2004 and Perrais et al., 2004.

claim: Capacitance measurements have shown that fusion pores initially flicker with conductances similar to those of large ion channels, before expanding irreversibly.
source: Capacitance measurements have shown that fusion pores initially flicker with conductances similar to those of large ion channels, before expanding irreversibly (Lollike et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lollike et al., 1995.

claim: Scission mechanisms involving dynamin can act even when the pore has dilated considerably beyond limit of reversible flicker behavior.
source: However, scission mechanisms involving dynamin can act even when the pore has dilated considerably beyond limit of reversible flicker behavior (Shin et al., 2018; Taraska and Almers, 2004; Zhao et al., 2016; Anantharam et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Relatively large granules retain their size during fusion-fission cycles.
source: even relatively large granules retain their size during fusion-fission cycles (MacDonald et al., 2006; Lollike et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to MacDonald et al., 2006 and Lollike et al., 1995.

claim: Separate mechanisms may operate for fusion pore regulation: one that prevents pore dilation by actively causing scission, and another by shifting the equilibrium between the open and closed states of the initial fusion pore.
source: Separate mechanisms may therefore operate, one that prevents pore dilation by actively causing scission, similar to the role of dynamins in endocytosis, and another by shifting the equilibrium between the open and closed states of the initial fusion pore.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Curvature-sensitive proteins are attractive candidates for fusion pore regulation since they could accumulate at the neck of the fused granule.
source: Curvature-sensitive proteins are particularly attractive for such roles since they could accumulate at the neck of the fused granule
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference.

claim: Ring-like assemblies have been observed for the Ca2+-sensor synaptotagmin.
source: such ring-like assemblies that have indeed been observed for the Ca2+-sensor synaptotagmin (Wang et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2001.

claim: Active pore dilation has been proposed to be driven by crowding of SNARE proteins.
source: Active pore dilation has also been proposed to be driven by crowding of SNARE proteins (Wu et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2017.

claim: Active pore dilation has been proposed to be driven by α-synuclein.
source: Active pore dilation has also been proposed to be driven by crowding of SNARE proteins (Wu et al., 2017) and α-synuclein (Logan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Logan et al., 2017.

claim: β-cell granules contain a variety of polypeptides (insulin, IAPP, chromogranins) and small molecule transmitter molecules (GABA, nucleotides, 5HT) that have important para- and autocrine functions within the islet.
source: β-cell granules contain a variety of polypeptides (insulin, IAPP, chromogranins) and small molecule transmitter molecules (GABA, nucleotides, 5HT) that have important para- and autocrine functions within the islet (Braun et al., 2012; Caicedo, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Braun et al., 2012 and Caicedo, 2013.

claim: Insulin modulates its own release by activating β-cell insulin receptors.
source: Insulin modulates its own release by activating β-cell insulin receptors (Leibiger et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Leibiger et al., 2008.

claim: Insulin stimulates somatostatin release.
source: Insulin modulates its own release by activating β-cell insulin receptors (Leibiger et al., 2008), stimulates somatostatin release (Vergari et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vergari et al., 2019.

claim: Insulin inhibits glucagon secretion.
source: Insulin modulates its own release by activating β-cell insulin receptors (Leibiger et al., 2008), stimulates somatostatin release (Vergari et al., 2019), and inhibits glucagon secretion (Ravier and Rutter, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ravier and Rutter, 2005.

claim: Insulin secretion is inhibited by IAPP/amylin and chromogranin cleavage products such as pancreastatin.
source: Insulin secretion is also inhibited by IAPP/amylin and chromogranin cleavage products such as pancreastatin (Braun et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Braun et al., 2012.

claim: GABA inhibits glucagon secretion from α-cells.
source: Of the small transmitters, GABA inhibits glucagon secretion from α-cells (Rorsman et al., 1989)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rorsman et al., 1989.

claim: GABA enhances insulin secretion.
source: Of the small transmitters, GABA inhibits glucagon secretion from α-cells (Rorsman et al., 1989) and enhances insulin secretion (Soltani et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Soltani et al., 2011.

claim: Tonic GABA signaling is important for the maintenance of β-cell mass.
source: tonic GABA signaling is important for the maintenance of β-cell mass (Soltani et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Soltani et al., 2011.

claim: Adenine nucleotides cause β-cell depolarization, intracellular Ca2+-release and enhanced insulin secretion.
source: Adenine nucleotides cause β-cell depolarization, intracellular Ca2+-release and enhanced insulin secretion (Khan et al., 2014; Jacques-Silva et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Khan et al., 2014 and Jacques-Silva et al., 2010.

claim: Adenine nucleotides also have negative effects on insulin secretion.
source: Adenine nucleotides cause β-cell depolarization, intracellular Ca2+-release and enhanced insulin secretion (Khan et al., 2014; Jacques-Silva et al., 2010), but also negative effects have been reported (Salehi et al., 2005; Poulsen et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Salehi et al., 2005 and Poulsen et al., 1999.

claim: Paracrine purinergic effects coordinate Ca2+ signaling among β-cells.
source: Paracrine purinergic effects also coordinate Ca2+ signaling among β-cells (Hellman et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hellman et al., 2004.

claim: Paracrine purinergic effects stimulate secretion of somatostatin from δ-cells.
source: Paracrine purinergic effects also coordinate Ca2+ signaling among β-cells (Hellman et al., 2004), stimulate secretion of somatostatin from δ-cells (Bertrand et al., 1990)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bertrand et al., 1990.

claim: Paracrine purinergic effects target islet vasculature and macrophages as part of the immune system.
source: Paracrine purinergic effects also coordinate Ca2+ signaling among β-cells (Hellman et al., 2004), stimulate secretion of somatostatin from δ-cells (Bertrand et al., 1990), and target islet vasculature and macrophages as part of the immune system (Weitz et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Weitz et al., 2018.

claim: By selectively allowing small molecule release, Epac/cAMP-dependent fusion pore restriction is expected to alter both the timing and the relative volume of peptidergic vs. transmitter signaling.
source: By selectively allowing small molecule release, Epac/cAMP-dependent fusion pore restriction is expected to alter both the timing and the relative volume of peptidergic vs. transmitter signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Even small delays between signals can be envisioned to affect the ratio of insulin to glucagon secretion.
source: Given that granule priming and islet electrical activity are regulated on a second time scale, even small delays between these signals can be envisioned to affect the ratio of insulin to glucagon secretion.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference.

claim: Epac-dependent fusion pore regulation may have profound consequences for islet physiology and glucose metabolism in vivo.
source: As illustrated by the recent finding of altered fusion pore behavior in type-2 diabetes (Collins et al., 2016), Epac-dependent fusion pore regulation may have profound consequences for islet physiology and glucose metabolism in vivo.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference and citation to Collins et al., 2016.
